data.title: Middle East Eye: Fighting in Yemen displaces 16,000 over past week: IOM
data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Fighting in Yemen displaces 16,000 over past week: IOM
The ongoing fighting in Yemen has displaced nearly 16,000 people the past week, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said Monday.
The UN agency indicated that 145,308 people (around 24,218 households) were displaced across eight governorates since insecurity escalated on the western coast in June
The total rose by 12 percent, or 15,870 people, between 21 to 28 September.
"Every week, we count thousands more people who have left everything behind,” said IOM’s chief of mission in Yemen Abdusattor Esoev.
"Behind these figures are parents trying to keep their children safe, older people who cannot travel far, and families who had very little to begin with."
"They need help now, and our response has to move as fast as they are,” he stressed, adding that families are in urgent need of shelter, food and protection.

data.author: Oscar Rickett
data.summary:
Council of Europe tells Serbia to implement judgement on Bahraini political prisoner
Submitted by

Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali was extradited from Serbia and has been in Bahrain's Jau Prison since 2022
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali has been held in Jau Prison since he was deported from Serbia in January 2022 (ADHRB)
Off
The Council of Europe has called on Serbia to implement a European Court of Human Rights judgement, which held that the Balkan country had violated the European Convention on Human Rights when it extradited a Bahraini activist seeking asylum.
Ahmed Jaafar Mohamed Ali travelled to Serbia to seek asylum in November 2021 but was arrested by authorities there based on an Interpol red notice, which Ali’s lawyers say was unlawfully issued.
The European Court of Human Rights issued an interim measure in January 2022 calling on Serbian authorities to refrain from extraditing Ali pending more information and particularly given the risk of torture or ill-treatment if he was returned.
Three days later, campaigners say a private plane, chartered by United Arab Emirates-based Royal Jet Airlines, took Ali to Bahrain.
Ever since then the activist, who fled Bahrain in 2011 and then lived in Iran before travelling to Serbia, has been held in Bahrain’s Jau Prison on two life sentences.
Inside the prison, Ali says he has been beaten, denied medical treatment, had his faith insulted and held in solitary confinement.
According to a recent call with fellow activists, a transcript of which was seen by Middle East Eye, Ali is currently being held in the prison’s Building Two, which houses violent offenders and those on serious drug charges.
Inside the building, the activist says these prisoners - acting on instruction from prison guards - beat and abuse him, creating a climate of fear that never lifts.

He also accused Tehran of using money received through sanctions relief or economic selling to build weapons and "export the revolution" rather than to "improve the lives of the Iranian people".

data.title: Middle East Eye: 'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide
data.author: Anuradha Bhasin
data.summary:
'Non-lethal': How India and Israel's brutal use of pellet guns spread worldwide
Submitted by
Anuradha Bhasin
on
Wed, 09/23/2026 - 11:36
The real danger isn't in how these lethal technologies, including pellet guns, are exported and shared; the greater peril is in the precedent their use against civilian protesters sets
Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) supporters wave national flags a day after the resignation of India's Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in Mumbai, India, 26 July 2026 (Punit Paranjape/AFP)
On
In July 2026, Amnesty International published a report Made in India: the supply of weapons and munitions to Israel. It found India shipped hundreds of thousands of weapon parts and munitions components to Israel throughout its Gaza offensive, and it warned the exports carry a "substantial risk" of contributing to what it calls Israel's "ongoing genocide".
The real danger isn't only in how these lethal technologies are exported and shared. The greater peril is in the wrong precedent their use against civilians sets.
A telling example is the use of pellet guns by police in Delhi to control a student’s march to the Indian parliament in protest against an examination leak scam, which injured at least 10 civilians, including a young man who may lose his vision forever.
The journey of the use of pellet guns for crowd control from Kashmir to New Delhi reminds us that any battleground is always a testing ground. What gets legitimised in one place does not stay there.
India introduced pellet guns in 2010 in Kashmir and framed it as a "non-lethal" or "less-lethal" weapon for crowd control. Between 2010 and 2019, 24 people were killed. Most casualties happened after their widespread use to control violent protests following the death of militant commander Burhan Wani, who was killed in an encounter in 2016. Between July 2016 and February 2019, metal pellets killed 18 people, blinded 139, and resulted in 2,942 injuries, of which 1,459 were serious eye injuries.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Araghchi adamant 'no change' in Iran's position, says conditions 'completely fair and reasonable'
data.author: Mera Aladam

Araghchi adamant 'no change' in Iran's position, says conditions 'completely fair and reasonable'
Iranian foreign minister Abbas Araghchi said that Tehran's conditions to the US are "completely fair and reasonable", adding that there has been no change in the country's position.
"There have been claims made for several hours now, and I can state with certainty that there has been no change in Iran's position," Araghchi told Iranian media.
He said that Tehran's conditions for the deal are "clear", including it stance on the opening of the Strait of Hormuz.
"Right now, it's just the issue of the Strait of Hormuz. The opening of the Strait of Hormuz is also subject to the fulfillment of the conditions that we announced to the other side," Araghchi said.
"There are conditions from the Supreme Leader, and these conditions must be implemented in order for the Strait of Hormuz to open, and our mission was to convey these conditions to both the American side and all other countries and the international community, so that they are aware that Iran has a plan in this regard.
"Iran's conditions are completely fair and reasonable, and if the Americans claim that they are seeking an agreement or a peaceful solution, we should introduce this solution."

data.author: Mera Aladam
data.summary:
Araghchi tells UN's Guterres that Iran will 'never stop demanding justice'
Iran's foreign minister told UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres that Tehran will "never stop demanding justice" against orchestrators of "war crimes", making reference to US and Israel.
Abbas Araghchi stressed to Guterres that Iran will continue to defend its national sovereignty and territorial integrity, adding that "the Iranian nation will never stop demanding justice and holding accountable and punishing the perpetrators and perpetrators of the US and Zionist war crimes".
"Iran has always been steadfast in using diplomatic tools to protect its national interests and ensure peace in the region, but the United States has repeatedly betrayed diplomacy over the past decade and, by breaking its promise, has caused insecurity in the region," he said.
The Iranian foreign minister also highlighted what he described as Israel's "genocide and war-mongering" in Palestine, Lebanon, Syria and other countries.
Araghchi pointed to these violations as a reminder to the UN and the Security Council of the "responsibility to end Israel's impunity and stop the crimes committed in Gaza and the West Bank".

Britain's Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband speaks on stage on the first day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, north-west England, on 27 September (AFP)
Off
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has confirmed the UK government is considering defying the Israeli order to close the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, saying “we do not want this to happen”.
The Israeli government ordered the closure of the consulate in retaliation for Miliband’s announcement of sanctions on illegal Israeli settlements earlier this month, giving Britain a deadline of 8 October.
It has previously been assumed that Britain would comply with this Israeli order, but Middle East Eye revealed on Monday that a final decision had not yet been made.
The consulate is in occupied Palestinian territory and Britain recognises the state of Palestine, meaning the UK government does not accept Israel’s order to close the consulate as legitimate.
Foreign Office officials gave an evasive response when approached on Monday morning asking for confirmation that Britain would close the consulate.
But Miliband addressed the issue in an interview with LBC later that day.
Asked whether the UK could refuse to close the consulate, the foreign secretary said: “We are looking at all our options on this.”

data.summary:
Miliband ‘looking at’ whether Palestine Action ban was sensible, argues mass arrests 'unintended'
Submitted by
Imran Mulla
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 08:47
Foreign secretary's remarks at Labour conference come after arrests made at protest against ban on the direct action group
Supporters of the proscribed group Palestine Action gather to protest outside the conference venue on the first day of the annual Labour Party conference in Liverpool, north-west England, on 27 September 2026 (AFP)
Off
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband has said the government is “looking at” whether the ban on Palestine Action as a terrorist organisation was politically sensible, arguing that the government had not intended for mass arrests to take place by implementing the proscription.
Miliband’s comments came at the Labour Party conference in Liverpool the day after the mass arrest of protesters against the ban outside the conference.
“I believe in the right to peaceful protest, I think that is important,” Miliband said in an interview on LBC on Tuesday.
Notably the foreign secretary avoided defending the ban on Palestine Action, which was introduced in the summer of 2025 under Keir Starmer’s premiership.
“On the specific issue of Palestine Action,” Miliband said, “there’s a case coming before the Supreme Court and so I’ll let that case play out, because I think it’s important that that court process takes its course.”
Pressed by interviewer Andrew Marr on whether he believed proscribing Palestine Action with “all those elderly people and vicars and grannies and so on" was politically sensible, Miliband responded: “I don’t think anyone’s intent was to have those people criminalised, but obviously the Supreme Court has got to look at this issue, and obviously it’s something we keep looking at as government.”
Speculation ban might be lifted
Miliband’s remarks have sparked speculation that the government might ultimately lift the ban on Palestine Action.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Israeli settlers set Palestinian homes and cars alight in West Bank rampage
data.author: MEE staff
data.summary:
Israeli settlers set Palestinian homes and cars alight in West Bank rampage
Submitted by
MEE staff
on
Tue, 09/29/2026 - 09:48
Large groups of attackers set fire to the Toubasi family’s homes in Jalud, forcing them to flee after earlier attacks aimed at taking over the property
A Palestinian man inspects a vehicle damaged in an Israeli settlers attack, in Al-Mughayyir, near Ramallah, in the occupied West Bank, 29 September (Reuters/Mohamad Torokman)
Off
Dozens of Israeli settlers rampaged through villages in the occupied West Bank overnight into Tuesday, attacking Palestinians and setting fire to homes and cars.
Around 100 settlers raided Jalud, south of Nablus, shortly after midnight on Monday, targeting the homes of the Toubasi family.
The family had been forced out of their home in July following repeated settler attacks aimed at taking over the property.
They returned to the house hours before Tuesday’s attack after an Israeli court ordered the army to secure their return.
Settlers then arrived in large numbers and set fire to two homes belonging to the Toubasi family, forcing them to flee again.
Mahmoud Toubasi, the owner of one of the houses, said the family was shocked by the extent of the destruction and vandalism when they returned.
The fire destroyed the house, damaged its contents and left it uninhabitable, he said.

Local media reported that Israeli forces eventually arrived but did not intervene to stop the attack. Instead, they provided protection to the settlers, according to the reports.
The Toubasi family was forced to evacuate the house again at gunpoint, the reports added.
The army also clashed with some settlers as it sought to disperse the large crowd.
Army officials said “rioters” had blocked roads, set tyres on fire and thrown stones at troops, injuring three officers.

data.title: Middle East Eye: Over 100 Israeli settlers raid Palestinian village, torch homes
data.author: Katherine Hearst
data.summary:
Over 100 Israeli settlers raid Palestinian village, torch homes
A mob of over 100 Israeli settlers raided a Palestinian village in the northern West Bank, setting fire to homes and vehicles.
Anadolu news agency reported that the pogrom took place as Israeli soldiers were accompanying a Palestinian family back to their home in Jalud after they had been displaced by settler attacks two months prior.
According to the report, settlers attacked the Toubasi family upon their arrival to their home.
Mahmoud al-Toubasi told AFP that, during the family's two month absence, Israeli settlers had occupied their home.
“My wife, my son and I went to the house in the car, accompanied by an army vehicle in front of us and another behind us,” he said.
